title: Food Webs and Interactions in Ecosystems
seo_title: Primary 6 Basic Science and Technology: Food Webs and Interactions in Ecosystems Worksheets
standard_code: Primary 6 Basic Science and Technology: Living and Non-Living Things
standard_text: Living things interact with each other (predation, competition, mutualism, commensalism, parasitism) and with abiotic factors; food webs show feeding relationships in an ecosystem. (summary of the Basic Science and Technology curriculum, Primary 6, theme: Living and Non-Living Things)
meta_desc: Free Primary 6 Basic Science and Technology worksheets (NERDC curriculum, theme: Living and Non-Living Things): biotic and abiotic factors, relationships between species, energy flow and cycles, food webs and change in ecosystems. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Energy flows through food webs; matter cycles; populations are limited by resources.
body_html:
How to think about it

An ecosystem is the living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts of an area and how they interact.

  • Symbiosis: mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits) and parasitism (one is harmed).
  • Only about 10% of the energy at one level passes to the next, so food chains are short.
  • Food, water, space and predators limit populations; succession slowly changes an ecosystem over time.
Example

A tick feeds on a cow. What relationship is this?

the tick benefits

the cow is harmed

Answer: parasitism

Example

Is sunlight biotic or abiotic?

it is not living

Answer: abiotic

Common mistakes

  • Thinking energy is recycled like matter (it flows one way).
  • Mixing up commensalism and mutualism.
  • Thinking populations can grow forever.

faq.q: What is the difference between biotic and abiotic factors?
faq.a: Biotic factors are living things. Abiotic factors are non-living, like sunlight, water and temperature.

faq.q: Why are there fewer top predators than producers?
faq.a: Energy is lost at each level, so there is less energy available for animals at the top.
The slow change in the plants and animals of an ecosystem over time, such as a burned forest growing back.

items.q: Femi observes that clownfish live in sea anemones and help keep them clean. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In mutualism, both benefit.

items.q: What is symbiosis?
c: a close relationship between two different species
items.e: It can be mutualism, commensalism or parasitism.

items.q: What is succession?
c: the gradual change in the species in an ecosystem over time
the life cycle of a frog
items.e: A field can slowly become a forest.

items.q: Which organisms recycle nutrients from dead matter back into the soil?
items.e: Fungi and bacteria are decomposers.

items.q: Bisi needs an example of predation (one organism hunts and eats another). Which is the best example?
c: a hermit crab lives in an empty snail shell
a mosquito feeds on a person's blood
weeds and corn take the same water
items.e: That is predation.

items.q: Cacti survive in deserts where it rarely rains. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Tolu needs an example of competition (organisms need the same limited resource). Which is the best example?
c: a lynx catches a snowshoe hare
a hawk dives for a rabbit
remora fish ride along with sharks and eat scraps
two kinds of birds eat the same insects
items.e: That is competition.

items.q: Kelechi observes that a hermit crab lives in an empty snail shell. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In commensalism, one benefits and the other is not helped or harmed.

items.q: Few plants grow on the dark floor of a dense rainforest. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Hauwa observes that fleas live on a cat. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In parasitism, one benefits and the other is harmed.

items.q: Zainab observes that moss grows on the bark of a tree. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In commensalism, one benefits and the other is not helped or harmed.

items.q: Mangrove trees grow in salty, waterlogged mud with little oxygen. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Fish in a pond die when the water becomes too acidic. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Why is only about 10% of energy passed on to the next level of a food chain?
c: Most energy is used for life processes or lost as heat.
items.e: This is shown in an energy pyramid.

items.q: Plants grow poorly in soil that lacks nitrates. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Nkechi observes that lice live on a person's head. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In parasitism, one benefits and the other is harmed.

items.q: Blessing observes that a frog eats a fly. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In predation, one organism hunts and eats another.

items.q: Corals die when sea water becomes too warm. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Fish gather near the surface of a pond with very little dissolved oxygen. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Seedlings grow towards a window. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Bees get nectar and flowers get pollinated. What kind of relationship is this?
items.e: Both species gain.

items.q: A bird nests in a tree and the tree is not affected. What kind of relationship is this?
items.e: One benefits; the other is not helped or harmed.

items.q: Aminat needs an example of mutualism (both benefit). Which is the best example?
c: a lynx catches a snowshoe hare
two male antelope fight over the same territory
fungi on plant roots get sugar and help roots take in water
items.e: That is mutualism.

items.q: What is the role of producers in an ecosystem?
c: They capture the Sun's energy and make food by photosynthesis.
items.e: Producers are at the base.

items.q: Head lice live on the human scalp and feed on blood. Which relationship is this?
items.e: The parasite benefits and the host is harmed.

items.q: Mistletoe takes water and minerals from the tree it grows on. Which relationship is this?
items.e: The parasite benefits and the host is harmed.

items.q: Ticks feed on the blood of a dog. Which relationship is this?
items.e: The parasite benefits and the host is harmed.

items.q: A shark hunts squid. Which relationship is this?
items.e: One organism hunts and eats the other.

items.q: Bacteria in a cow's gut digest cellulose; the bacteria get food and shelter. Which relationship is this?
items.e: Both organisms benefit.

items.q: Bees collect nectar from flowers and pollinate them. Which relationship is this?
items.e: Both organisms benefit.

items.q: A kingfisher catches and eats mudskippers. Which relationship is this?
items.e: One organism hunts and eats the other.

items.q: Kemi observes weeds and tomato plants using water and nutrients in a garden. What is happening?
items.e: When organisms need the same limited resource, they compete.

items.q: Which is a biotic factor?
items.e: Biotic means living.

items.q: Tobi observes trout in a crowded stream using food and space. What is happening?
items.e: When organisms need the same limited resource, they compete.

items.q: Long-tailed macaques and squirrels both eat the same fruits in a forest. Which relationship is this?
items.e: Both need the same limited resource.

items.q: Oxpecker birds eat ticks off the backs of buffalo. Which relationship is this?
items.e: Both organisms benefit.

items.q: Lichen is made of a fungus and an alga; the alga makes food and the fungus holds water. Which relationship is this?
items.e: Both organisms benefit.

items.q: Ruth needs an example of commensalism (one benefits and the other is not helped or harmed). Which is the best example?
c: cattle egrets eat insects stirred up by grazing cows
lice live on a person's head
mistletoe takes water and nutrients from a tree
bees get nectar from flowers and carry pollen between them
items.e: That is commensalism.

items.q: Nkechi needs an example of commensalism (one benefits and the other is not helped or harmed). Which is the best example?
c: a tapeworm lives in an animal's intestine
lice live on a person's head
barnacles ride on a whale without hurting it
bacteria in your intestines get food and help you digest
items.e: That is commensalism.

items.q: Simi observes two kinds of birds using insects in the same trees. What is happening?
items.e: When organisms need the same limited resource, they compete.

Where does most of the energy taken in by the insect go?
c: All of it passes to the shrew.
It is used for life processes and lost as heat, not passed on.
items.e: Only about 10% passes on.

items.q: In this mangrove food web, what is the role of the kingfisher?
c: a consumer that eats other animals
items.e: Look at what it eats in the web.

items.q: Primary consumers take in 1,000 kJ from producers but pass only 100 kJ to secondary consumers. Where does most of the rest go?
c: It is used in respiration for life processes and lost as heat.
It is recycled back to the producers.
It is stored in the Sun.
items.e: Energy flows through a food chain and is not recycled.

items.q: Kelechi's energy pyramid shows 50,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 50,000 → 5,000 → 500.

items.q: Hadiza's energy pyramid shows 20,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the primary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 20,000 → 2,000.

items.q: Producers in a food chain trap 20,000 kJ of energy. About 10% passes to each next level. How much reaches the secondary consumers?
Halima's energy pyramid shows 5,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the primary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 5,000 → 500.

items.q: Obinna's energy pyramid shows 2,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 2,000 → 200 → 20.

items.q: Bisi's energy pyramid shows 10,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the primary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 10,000 → 1,000.

items.q: Fatima's energy pyramid shows 10,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10.

items.e: It makes its own food by photosynthesis.

Uju's energy pyramid shows 5,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?

items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 20,000 → 2,000 → 200 → 20.

items.q: Producers in a food chain trap 50,000 kJ of energy. About 10% passes to each next level. How much reaches the secondary consumers?
Babatunde's energy pyramid shows 2,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 2,000 → 200 → 20 → 2.

items.q: Esther's energy pyramid shows 1,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 1,000 → 100 → 10.

items.q: Producers in a food chain trap 100,000 kJ of energy. About 10% passes to each next level. How much energy reaches the primary consumers?
Producers in a food chain trap 10,000 kJ of energy. About 10% passes to each next level. How much reaches the secondary consumers?
In Nonso's mangrove food web, which organism level holds the most energy?
c: the producers, such as mangrove trees
items.e: Producers capture energy from sunlight; each level up has less.

items.q: Use the pond food web. Which of these is food for the snail?
items.e: The arrow goes from the water lettuce to the snail, so the snail eats water lettuce.

items.q: Use the school garden food web. How many kinds of food does the grasshopper eat in this web?
items.e: Count the arrows pointing to the grasshopper: grass.

items.q: Use the mangrove swamp food web. Which animal eats the mangrove tree?
items.e: An arrow goes from the mangrove tree to the crab.

items.q: Use the coral reef food web. How many kinds of food does the parrotfish eat in this web?
items.e: Count the arrows pointing to the parrotfish: seaweed.

items.q: This is a mangrove swamp food web. In this web, the heron's food is: mudskipper. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: It eats only animals.

items.q: This is a coral reef food web. In this web, the zooplankton's food is: phytoplankton. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: It eats only plants (producers).

items.q: Where does the energy in almost every food chain come from first?
items.e: Plants use the Sun's energy to make food.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. In this web, the zooplankton eats phytoplankton. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: Herbivores eat only plants, carnivores only animals, omnivores both.

items.q: Use the pond food web. What does the dragonfly eat?
items.e: The arrow goes from the mosquito larva to the dragonfly, so the dragonfly eats a mosquito larva.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Most of the coral trout are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the coral trout eats small fish in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Look at the pond food web. Which animal eats the snail?
items.e: An arrow goes from the snail to the frog.

items.q: Look at the pond food web. Which animal eats the algae?
items.e: An arrow goes from the algae to the small fish.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Which organism is not eaten by any other organism in this web?
items.e: No arrow leaves the green turtle.

items.q: Look at the coral reef food web. Which of these is food for the shark?
items.e: The arrow goes from the squid to the shark, so the shark eats a squid.

items.q: This is a coral reef food web. Which animal eats the squid?
items.e: An arrow goes from the squid to the shark.

items.q: Look at the school garden food web. How many kinds of food does the garden lizard eat in this web?
items.e: Count the arrows pointing to the garden lizard: spider, grasshopper.

items.q: Look at the pond food web. In this web, the snail's food is: algae, water lettuce. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: It eats only plants (producers).

items.q: Use the pond food web. Which animal eats the frog?
items.e: An arrow goes from the frog to the heron.

items.q: Look at the mangrove swamp food web. Which of these is food for the mudskipper?
items.e: The arrow goes from the algae to the mudskipper, so the mudskipper eats algae.

items.q: Use the school garden food web. In this web, the snake's food is: mynah, garden lizard. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: It eats only animals.

items.q: Why do scientists study interactions before bringing a new species into an area?
c: The new species may compete with, eat or harm native species.
items.e: Predicting interactions prevents problems.

items.q: Bola reads: “A long drought dries up streams.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Ikenna studies a burned forest recovering over many years. Which stage comes after “bare soil or rock”?
items.e: This gradual recovery is called succession.

items.q: Nonso reads: “A volcano covers land with ash.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Uju watches an abandoned farm field over 50 years. What process is changing the field from grasses to forest?
items.e: Communities change over time after a disturbance.

items.q: Gbenga graphs barn owls and mice on a farm. When mice increase, owls increase a year later. Why?
c: More food (mice) supports more owl chicks.
items.e: Predators follow prey.

items.q: Ibrahim reads: “A flood covers a river valley with mud.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Bisi studies a burned forest recovering over many years. Which stage comes after “grasses and wildflowers”?
items.e: This gradual recovery is called succession.

items.q: By how much did frogs decrease from 2015 to 2019 in Peter's data?
Ruth finds that cowbirds lay eggs in other birds' nests, and the other birds raise the cowbird chicks. What kind of relationship is this?
items.e: The host birds are harmed.

items.q: Victor's graph shows frogs in a lake area. A fungus disease arrived in 2016. Which claim does the data support?
c: The graph shows the arrival caused growth.
The number of frogs declined after a fungus disease arrived.
The number of frogs grew after a fungus disease arrived.
items.e: The numbers drop after 2016.

items.q: Dayo reads: “Kudzu vines spread over forests in the South.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Nkechi removes the ants from some acacia trees. Those trees get eaten more by animals. What does this show?
c: The ants and trees have a mutualism that protects the tree.
items.e: Evidence for a mutualism.

items.q: Ife reads: “Hunters remove most of the sea otters from a coast.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Abdullahi studies a burned forest recovering over many years. Which stage comes after “shrubs and small trees”?
items.e: This gradual recovery is called succession.

items.q: Hauwa's graph shows songbirds in a lake area. Outdoor cats arrived in 2016. Which claim does the data support?
c: The number of songbirds grew after outdoor cats arrived.
The graph shows the arrival caused growth.
The number of songbirds declined after outdoor cats arrived.
items.e: The numbers drop after 2016.

items.q: Zainab's graph shows native plants in a lake area. An invasive vine arrived in 2016. Which claim does the data support?
c: The native plants population declined after an invasive vine arrived.
The graph shows the arrival caused growth.
The native plants population grew after an invasive vine arrived.
items.e: The numbers drop after 2016.

items.q: Yetunde reads: “A cold snap freezes a lake for months.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Funke's graph shows native fish in a lake area. An invasive fish arrived in 2016. Which claim does the data support?
c: The native fish population declined after an invasive fish arrived.
The native fish population grew after an invasive fish arrived.
The graph shows the arrival caused growth.
items.e: The numbers drop after 2016.

items.q: Two species of barnacles live on the same rock. When one is removed, the other spreads into its area. What does this show?
items.e: Removing a competitor frees resources.
